name: Pinswang
kurzbeschreibung: Charming village on the border with Bavaria, home to the legendary Schloss and the royal Königsschlösser neighborhood.
text:
Overview

Pinswang is situated in the northern sector of the district of Reutte in the Außerfern region at an altitude of 824 metres, nestled directly against the Bavarian border in the famed Füssen Königswinkel area. This charming agricultural village is home to approximately 420 residents and covers an area of 9.4 square kilometres, divided into the two scenic hamlets of Unterpinswang and Oberpinswang. Tucked into a wide basin at the base of Mount Kienberg and the Schluxen forest along the banks of the Lech River gravel plains, Pinswang directly borders the Bavarian towns of Füssen and Schwangau. Although world-renowned royal landmarks such as Neuschwanstein and Hohenschwangau Castles lie virtually in sight and within walking distance, Pinswang has carefully preserved complete rural tranquility, farming traditions, and local heritage. The landscape is characterized by lush alpine meadows, dense beech forests, and the dramatic backdrop of the Allgäu and Ammergau Alps.

History

Settlement history here reaches back into antiquity, encouraged by the proximity of the Roman Via Claudia Augusta. The community was first documented in 1095 under the name Puncinwanc. Perched high above the Vils Valley on a forested rocky ridge stands the Vilsegg Castle ruins: erected around 1220 by the noble Lords of Hohenegg, this Staufer-era fortress ranks among Tyrol's most significant medieval strongholds, distinguished by its massive stone keep. International historical renown belongs to the Gutshof Schluxen estate in Unterpinswang: situated along the historic Fürstenstraße (Princes' Road) constructed in 1838 by Crown Prince Maximilian of Bavaria, this estate received a tavern license in 1853 and became the cherished resting stop of King Ludwig II of Bavaria and Queen Marie during carriage journeys between Hohenschwangau and Reutte. The original Fürstenstube parlour still showcases a tiled stove presented as a royal gift by King Ludwig II. The Baroque Parish Church of St. Ulrich was built in 1725–1729 by court architect Franz Xaver Kleinhans.

Getting There

Pinswang benefits from exceptional toll-free access from neighbouring Bavaria. Motorists arriving from Germany take motorway A7 to its terminus at Füssen or cross the border at Füssen/Ziegelwies, reaching Pinswang in just five to seven minutes; from the south, federal road B179 leads via Reutte and Musau directly to the village. Rail passengers can use Füssen railway station in Germany (approx. 5 km away, with direct regional trains to Munich and Augsburg) or the stations of Reutte in Tirol, Musau, and Ulrichsbrücke-Füssen on the Außerfern Railway. VVT bus route 100 runs regular connections linking Füssen and Reutte with Unterpinswang and Oberpinswang. Cyclists can pedal effortlessly along the riverside trails of the Lech Cycle Route.

Tips

An unforgettable scenic and historical hike is the royal circular route: starting from Gutshof Schluxen, walk in the footsteps of King Ludwig II along the Fürstenstraße through silent mountain forests towards Lake Alpsee, continuing directly to Hohenschwangau and Neuschwanstein Castles and returning past Lake Schwansee. Another rewarding excursion is the walk up to Vilsegg Castle ruins, where the medieval keep offers expansive panoramas across the alpine foothills. Art enthusiasts should step inside the Parish Church of St. Ulrich to admire the Baroque central design by master architect Franz Kleinhans and its ceiling frescoes depicting the Battle of Lechfeld. Nature lovers will enjoy exploring the protected Lech River wetlands or visiting the nearby Forest Experience Centre Ziegelwies featuring its treetop canopy walkway.
